cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-64-christ.summary: The composition is a great circle formed by the signs of the zodiac, 'the outgoings of the morning and evening', with sun and moon. Within it rises a mountain girded by walls, and on its summit the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos with a cross-staff and angels treads on a lion and an adder. The drawing turns a harvest psalm into an image of Christ as Lord of the whole ordered cosmos.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-64-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-benedictus-nati.summary: At the left is the Nativity: before a domed building, the 'house of David', the Virgin reclines on a bed with Joseph seated beside her, while two midwives bathe the Christ child in a large bowl and angels fly down with napkins. In the centre Zacharias lays his hand on the head of the young John the Baptist, and in the heavens a half-figure of the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos appears in a mandorla among angels holding the 'horn of salvation'. The Benedictus was sung daily at Lauds.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-benedictus-nati.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:monumental-tokali-calling-peter-andr.summary: Christ, haloed and robed, strides towards the shore of a blue sea in which two boats carry pairs of fishermen; the upper boat holds Peter and Andrew, the lower James and John. At the left, part of another scene with a building and a seated haloed figure is visible. Christ's outstretched hand calls the fishermen from their nets to become his disciples.
facts: Tokalı Kilise ('Church of the Buckle'), the largest church at Göreme, comprises an Old Church of the 10th century, painted in strips of red and green, and a larger New Church of the late 10th or early 11th century whose walls are dominated by rich indigo blue made from lapis lazuli.

Wikipedia notes that the lapis lazuli used in the New Church alone has been estimated as worth some 31.5 pounds of gold; the donors are often thought to have been the Phokas family, though without firm evidence.

cur:monumental-tokali-calling-peter-andr.notes: The photograph shows a detail of the wall; whether the scene belongs to the Old or the New Church is not stated in the source. Dates for both phases are debated (c. 910s–920s for the Old Church; mid-10th to early 11th century for the New).

cur:objects2-cma-resist-dyed-hanging.summary: This fragile linen hanging, its blue resist-dyed pattern now worn and fragmentary, once told biblical stories in registers. According to the museum, the upper register shows the Virgin with the Christ Child on a cross-legged stool while the Magi approach with gifts, identified by a Coptic inscription; the middle register may show the Baptism of Christ and the Multiplication of the Loaves and Fishes, and below Jonah is swallowed by the sea monster. Such hangings brought the Gospel into the homes and churches of Christian Egypt.
facts: The cloth was decorated by resist-dyeing: areas protected by a paste or wax stayed undyed when the fabric was dipped in indigo, leaving the figures in light outline.
The museum notes that a Coptic inscription identifies the three kings approaching the Virgin and Child.
cur:objects2-cma-resist-dyed-hanging.notes: The museum itself marks the Baptism identification as uncertain ('may depict').
